h1: Hallertau Tradition hops for classic lager aroma on a budget
title: Hallertau Tradition Hops for Lager Aroma | Craft Beer School
desc: What Hallertau Tradition hops bring to a lager, how they compare with Mittelfrüh and how to dose them for classic German aroma.
teaser: Hallertau Tradition gives you most of the classic German lager aroma from a hardier plant that is easier to buy.
standfirst: Hallertau Tradition was bred to give lager brewers the soft floral aroma of the old Hallertau landrace without its weak spots in the field. For a brewer importing hops into India, that makes it one of the most practical noble type choices.
sections: Tradition was bred to keep the old aroma alive

Hallertauer Mittelfrüh is the landrace behind much of what people mean by German lager aroma. It is also a fussy plant with low yields and poor resistance to verticillium wilt. In the early 1990s the Hüll hop research centre in Bavaria released Hallertauer Tradition, bred to keep that aroma while growing better.

The result is an aroma hop with alpha acid around 5 to 7%, a little higher than Mittelfrüh. Most tasters describe its profile as floral, herbal and grassy with a light spice. In a finished helles or pils, few drinkers would pick them apart without a side by side tasting.
Why it suits a tighter hop budget

We will not quote prices, because hop prices move every harvest and every importer is different. The logic is structural. A variety that yields more per hectare and loses fewer plants to disease is easier for growers to produce reliably. That usually makes Tradition easier to secure in volume and on contract than a scarce landrace.

The higher alpha also helps. At 6% alpha against 4%, you need roughly a third less hop weight for the same bitterness from a given addition. On a 1,000 litre brewpub batch that difference shows up in the hop line of your cost sheet every single brew.
How to dose it in a pils or a helles

Tradition works as a single hop in a German lager, carrying both bitterness and aroma. A simple pattern for a 1,000 litre helles at around 18 IBU:

  • 60 minute addition for about 14 IBU. At 6% alpha and 28% utilisation that is 14 x 1,000 / (0.06 x 0.28 x 1,000), or about 830 g.
  • 10 minute addition of around 0.5 g per litre, so 500 g, for aroma. It adds a little bitterness too, so taste before you push it.

For a pils in the 22 to 40 IBU range, raise the bittering charge and keep the late addition near 1 g per litre. Some brewers add a short whirlpool rest at about 80 °C instead of a late boil addition, which keeps more of the floral oil.
How it compares with its neighbours

Against Mittelfrüh, Tradition is a touch grassier and slightly less refined, but very close. Against Hallertau Hersbrucker, it is less hay like and a little more bitter. Against American grown aroma hops bred to imitate Hallertau, such as Crystal, it is milder and more floral, with less of the woody spice.

For a recipe that just says "Hallertau", Tradition is a safe interpretation. For a recipe that names Mittelfrüh specifically and is entered in competition, brew one batch of each before you substitute.
Aroma hops suffer most in the heat

Bittering hops forgive a little abuse. Aroma hops do not. The oils that give Tradition its floral character are volatile and oxidise quickly once a foil is opened. A pellet that smells of cheese or wet cardboard has lost the very thing you bought it for.

Keep the foil sealed and frozen at around minus 18 °C, buy in quantities you will finish within a few months of opening and rub a few pellets between your fingers before each brew. Fresh Tradition smells of flowers and cut grass. If it smells flat, use it for bittering and open a new bag for the late addition.

Working out why one batch of lager smells brighter than another, at the same recipe, is where hop chemistry starts to pay for itself.
Adjunct lagers show hop aroma more clearly

Many lagers brewed in India use rice or maize for a quarter or more of the grist. Those adjuncts add fermentable sugar without much malt flavour, so the finished beer is lighter in body and has less bready sweetness to cover the hops. A late addition that sits quietly in an all malt helles can stand out in a rice lager.

That is a good thing if you want a crisp, lightly floral beer. Tradition suits it well. Start the late addition lower than you would in an all malt beer, around 0.3 to 0.5 g per litre. Work upwards batch by batch. Bitterness also reads sharper in a thinner beer, so a rice lager at 18 IBU can taste sharper than an all malt lager at the same number. Our guide to clean German lager in an Indian brewpub covers the rest of the process side.

If you brew a German style lager with a mix of hops today, try one batch with Hallertau Tradition doing all of it: a 60 minute charge and a late addition from the same lot. Taste it next to your usual beer at the same IBU. You will learn more about what the hop does from that one comparison than from any supplier sheet.
faqs: Is Hallertau Tradition a noble hop?
Strictly, no. The noble label usually covers the old landraces such as Hallertau Mittelfrüh, Tettnang, Spalt and Saaz. Tradition is a modern variety bred to share that aroma.
What alpha acid does Hallertau Tradition have?
It typically measures about 5 to 7% alpha acid, slightly higher than Hallertau Mittelfrüh.
In most German lagers, yes, with very little difference in the glass. Adjust the weight for its higher alpha and taste the two side by side if the recipe matters to you.
